title: Sparrow AI - relevance ops & hosting options (discovery)
summary: Initial discovery focused on embedding dimensionality tradeoffs, rerank placement, and whether to run on Hosted, Dedicated, or Private. Sparrow wants a pilot to validate throughput at 75-150 QPS with top-k vector fanout + neural rerank. Action items: send security pack, pricing for 3-month pilot, and pilot test plan.

transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-04-18
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Ethan Ross (CTO - Sparrow AI), Priya Kumar (Lead ML Eng), Luis Ortega (Infra), Zoe Chen (PM)
Shared artifacts: deck: https://redwood.ai/decks/sparrow-pilot-v1.pdf, benchmark sheet: https://sheets.goo.gl/benchmark-sparrow, security packet: (will share)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan Hayes (Redwood): Hey everybody, thanks for carving out the time. Quick intros then we'll jump into your current stack and goals.
[00:18] Ethan Ross (Sparrow): Hi all, Ethan here. We're trying to figure out where to run embeddings + rerank, do we host with Redwood hosted API, buy dedicated pools, or go private in our VPC. Primary asks are throughput and predictable tail latency.
[00:35] Jordan Hayes (Redwood): Great, that aligns. Maya, do you want to walk through typical hosting tradeoffs?
[00:40] Maya Patel (Redwood): Sure. So, hosted gives fastest time-to-value — you get the API, model catalog, and streaming. Dedicated gives predictable throughput and reserved GPU pools which is helpful for stable QPS. Private adds VPC peering, KMS/HSM, and audit log controls. We often see customers start hosted and then flip to dedicated for the pilot if they need consistent 95th pct latency.
[01:10] Priya Kumar (Sparrow): Our rough target is 75 QPS sustained for user-facing search, occasionally spiking to 150 QPS. In production we'd like P50 < 60ms and P95 < 250ms for the full retrieval + rerank path. Are those realistic?
[01:34] Maya Patel (Redwood): Yes, but depends on design. If you do vector fanout top-50 from the VDB and then a neural rerank call per candidate, that can multiply inference cost and latency. We recommend reranking on a compact candidate set (top-10) or running a light-weight cross-encoder on dedicated GPUs. Also caching prefix KV can shave a lot if queries repeat.
[02:05] Luis Ortega (Sparrow): We're using Milvus in prod today and have some index sharding. How does Redwood integrate — do you push embeddings into our DB or host embeddings and push vectors?
[02:22] Liam O'Connor (Redwood): Good question. We support both models: you can compute embeddings with our hosted model and push to your VDB, or host the whole inference pipeline on Redwood and only store vectors in your DB. For Private deployment we can run within your VPC so vectors never traverse public internet. There are slight transcription notes — sometimes 'Redwood Dedicate' in our docs is shortened — sorry for the audio artifact.
[02:50] Ethan Ross (Sparrow): If we compute embeddings on Redwood hosted and push to Milvus, is there an egress cost or encryption-at-rest concern?
[03:03] Maya Patel (Redwood): For hosted there's egress but it's usually small; for strict compliance you should use Private. We support KMS for key management and can route logs to your SIEM. We'll share the security pack.
[03:24] Zoe Chen (Sparrow): What about dimensionality — our current pipeline uses 1536-d vectors. But we saw a paper that 768 dims with a reranker matches most of our use cases and reduces storage/cost. Thoughts?
[03:38] Maya Patel (Redwood): 1536 gives richness but doubles storage and index fanout cost vs 768. Often the sweet spot is 512-1024 for throughput-sensitive systems, then rely on a neural reranker to recover precision. We'll run a dimension sweep in the pilot. Priya, do you have constraints on latency vs recall?
[03:57] Priya Kumar (Sparrow): We can't sacrifice critical recall for legal docs — recall must be high for compliance search. But for product search we can accept some drop if latency is better. So we want per-route policies.
[04:12] Jordan Hayes (Redwood): That's exactly where routing policies help — you can route sensitive traffic to Private (higher-quality model, more dims) and public product queries to a cost-optimized path.
[04:26] Ethan Ross (Sparrow): Can you explain more about the rerank placement — do you run it before or after vector DB scoring?
[04:34] Maya Patel (Redwood): Typically flow is embed -> VDB ANN -> lightweight re-score -> neural rerank on top-k. Lightweight re-score can be dot-product or simple lexical overlap. Then neural rerank is a cross-encoder or a small LLM that takes the query+candidate batch. If you do rerank for top-50 it's more expensive; top-10 is common.
[05:02] Luis Ortega (Sparrow): For throughput testing, what metrics should we collect?
[05:09] Liam O'Connor (Redwood): Capture QPS, p50/p95/p99 latency for retrieval and rerank, GPU utilization, batch sizes, and per-token cost if applicable. We'll provide a bench plan.
[05:25] Priya Kumar (Sparrow): Do you support quantized embeddings? We saw references to 8-bit quant and int4 for models — will that help?
[05:36] Maya Patel (Redwood): Yes, quantization helps memory and throughput for the embedding model itself, but for vector similarity you generally store full-precision or IVFPQ compressed vectors in the VDB. Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles per workload. There's some artifact where the transcript autoparsed 'quantizashun' — ignore that.
[05:55] Zoe Chen (Sparrow): Regarding private deployment, what's the typical timeline and what infra do we need?
[06:04] Jordan Hayes (Redwood): For Private: initial setup 2-4 weeks for network and certs, full on-prem or air-gapped goes longer. We need VPC peering, a bastion for ops, and KMS/HSM for keys. We'll send a checklist.
[06:20] Ethan Ross (Sparrow): How do rollouts work? If we pin a model version, can we do canary?
[06:25] Maya Patel (Redwood): Yes, Redwood supports canary rollouts, A/B tests, and automatic fallback to a cheaper variant if latency or errors spike. That helps during pilot scale-ups.
[06:38] Priya Kumar (Sparrow): What's the unit economics if we compare hosted vs dedicated? Rough numbers ok.
[06:44] Jordan Hayes (Redwood): Hosted is pay-per-use; good for low to variable volume. Dedicated has a monthly commit but lower per-token (or per-inference) unit costs and reserved capacity which hits predictability. For your 75-150 QPS sustained, dedicated often ends up cheaper if you want consistent P95. We'll include a sample cost model in the SOW.
[07:06] Luis Ortega (Sparrow): For Milvus sharded indexes, how does Redwood handle fanout? Do you coordinate with their shards?
[07:15] Liam O'Connor (Redwood): We treat the VDB as a black box for ANN queries; you can either query from your app directly or we can orchestrate fanout in the Redwood runtime for hybrid search. If you want cross-shard aggregation we can support parallel queries and merge results — there are tradeoffs for tail latency.
[07:34] Ethan Ross (Sparrow): We also have a legal team asking about audit logs and retention — are logs accessible?
[07:41] Maya Patel (Redwood): Yes, audit logs with RBAC and retention policies. For Private you can ship logs to your SIEM; for hosted we provide API-level audit exports and redwood console views.
[07:53] Zoe Chen (Sparrow): Any concerns about data residency? We have users in EU and US.
[07:58] Jordan Hayes (Redwood): You can pin region routing so EU data stays in EU regions. Private gives more control. We'll note the geography constraints in the SOW.
[08:12] Priya Kumar (Sparrow): For the pilot I'd like to test two flows: A) Redwood-hosted embeddings -> Milvus in our infra -> rerank in Red wood dedicated; B) Full private deployment with embeddings and rerank in our VPC. Can we scope both?
[08:28] Maya Patel (Redwood): Yes, we can. Pilot A is faster to spin up; Pilot B will validate compliance and private networking. We'll propose metrics and a 4-week timeline for A, 6-8 weeks for B.
[08:40] Ethan Ross (Sparrow): Will we be able to run bench with 200k sample docs?
[08:45] Liam O'Connor (Redwood): Yep. If you share sample S3 we can run distributed ingest and simulate production patterns, spikes, and tail latency.
[08:55] Priya Kumar (Sparrow): On rerank models, do you provide out-of-the-box cross-encoders or do we bring our own fine-tuned model?
[09:04] Maya Patel (Redwood): Both. We have curated models in the catalog and support custom model uploads. For private you can bring bespoke models; for hosted we can host your model with model pinning.
[09:16] Zoe Chen (Sparrow): Our team wants to understand failure modes — e.g., if dedicated pool runs out of capacity, what's fallback?
[09:23] Jordan Hayes (Redwood): Redwood supports automatic fallback to a compatible hosted variant or routing to another region. You can configure policy per route. Also we have circuit breakers and rate limits.
[09:34] Ethan Ross (Sparrow): Any guidance on batch size for rerank to hit latency targets?
[09:40] Liam O'Connor (Redwood): For rerank, small batches (8-16) keep latency low on GPUs; bigger batches increase throughput but raise tail latency. For your P95 target, start with batch 8 and tune.
[09:54] Priya Kumar (Sparrow): For the VDB, would it make sense to down-sample dims from 1536 to 768 and rely more on rerank?
[10:02] Maya Patel (Redwood): Yes, that's a common pattern. We'll include a dimension sweep (1536, 1024, 768, 512) and measure recall/latency/cost tradeoffs.
[10:15] Zoe Chen (Sparrow): Are there examples of other customers in our space?
[10:18] Jordan Hayes (Redwood): We have retail and legal customers who've done similar splits. We'll anonymize case studies and share throughput numbers.
[10:25] Ethan Ross (Sparrow): On security, are you SOC2 Type II?
[10:29] Maya Patel (Redwood): Yes, we are SOC2 Type II. We'll share the certs and the compliance pack after the call.
[10:36] Priya Kumar (Sparrow): For pilot acceptance, what are typical success criteria?
[10:41] Liam O'Connor (Redwood): Usually: 1) meet P95 latency target for retrieval+rerank under load; 2) maintain recall delta below X% vs baseline on eval queries; 3) validate ops runbook (alerts, logs, rollback). We'll propose specific thresholds in SOW.
[11:00] Zoe Chen (Sparrow): Any initial blockers?
[11:03] Priya Kumar (Sparrow): We need to confirm legal sign-off for data transfer for pilot A. Also resource to provision S3.
[11:09] Jordan Hayes (Redwood): Noted. We'll include legal contacts and sample DPA.
[11:15] Ethan Ross (Sparrow): How will we measure recall for compliance docs specifically?
[11:20] Maya Patel (Redwood): We'll use labeled relevance sets and run batch evals; Redwood Optimize can track regressions against golden prompt sets.
[11:34] Luis Ortega (Sparrow): If we need sub-100ms rerank P95, is that feasible?
[11:39] Liam O'Connor (Redwood): For small top-k and a compact rerank model on dedicated GPUs, yes. But if you want neural rerank on 50 candidates it gets harder. We can profile.
[11:52] Priya Kumar (Sparrow): Can we get a sample config that shows the network flow for pilot A?
[11:58] Jordan Hayes (Redwood): We'll attach an architecture diagram in the next email.
[12:05] Ethan Ross (Sparrow): Are there throttles or quotas for hosted embedding generation?
[12:10] Maya Patel (Redwood): There are rate limits on hosted tiers; dedicated removes shared limits and gives reserved capacity. We'll map quotas to your SLOs in the SOW.
[12:22] Zoe Chen (Sparrow): For Private, what about on-prem GPU compatibility — do you support different GPU types?
[12:28] Liam O'Connor (Redwood): Yes. The runtime has kernel selection for different GPU architectures; we'll advise on the optimal instance types based on sequence length and model size.
[12:40] Priya Kumar (Sparrow): Let's talk about costs for storing vectors — say 200k docs at 1536 dims float32 is... expensive. Any compression suggestions?
[12:49] Maya Patel (Redwood): Use IVFPQ or OPQ in the VDB to compress and reduce disk; also consider lower-dim embeddings. We'll provide a storage-cost estimate in the cost model.
[13:03] Jordan Hayes (Redwood): Quick show of hands on pilots: do you want to run both A and B in parallel or start with A and then expand?
[13:10] Ethan Ross (Sparrow): Start A first, but kick off architect work for B in parallel. Legal needs to review data flow while engineering works on S3 sample.
[13:20] Priya Kumar (Sparrow): Timeline feel: pilot A in 4 weeks, pilot B in 6-8. That works.
[13:27] Zoe Chen (Sparrow): For the bench plan, can Redwood simulate mixed traffic patterns? We have spikes and tail heavy.
[13:33] Liam O'Connor (Redwood): Yes, we'll simulate steady-state and burst traffic and report p50/p95/p99.
[13:42] Luis Ortega (Sparrow): Any API changes on our side if we use hosted embedding vs private?
[13:47] Maya Patel (Redwood): Minimal. If you compute embeddings in-hosted then push to Milvus via your pipeline, you only need to change the embedding call. For private, we might host a model endpoint in your VPC.
[14:02] Jordan Hayes (Redwood): Ok, let's recap and outline next steps — Maya?
[14:07] Maya Patel (Redwood): Recap: 1) Redwood to send security pack and SOC2 artifacts. 2) SE to send pilot SOW and bench plan (we will include dimension sweep and 75/150 QPS tests). 3) Sparrow to provide sample S3 bucket and legal contacts. 4) Schedule pilot kickoff. Links: deck and bench sheet are in the chat.
[14:29] Zoe Chen (Sparrow): That's helpful. One last question — do you offer managed ops during pilot (pager escalation)?
[14:36] Jordan Hayes (Redwood): Yes, we can provide managed on-call as an add-on for the pilot. We'll include that option in the SOW.
[14:45] Ethan Ross (Sparrow): Great. Anything else from Redwood?
[14:48] Maya Patel (Redwood): We'll also include suggested model variants (512/768/1536), recommended batch sizes for rerank, and a fallback routing policy for capacity events.
[15:00] Priya Kumar (Sparrow): Thanks — we'll get S3 access and legal contact this week.
[15:05] Jordan Hayes (Redwood): Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the SOW and security pack by end of day Thursday.

End of transcript
